name: The Nestorian controversy (two Persons vs. one)
plain_explanation: A theological dispute over whether Christ was really two separate persons -- one human, one divine -- joined together, or a single, unified person.
precise_definition: The Christological dispute, chiefly between Nestorius and Cyril, over whether Christ's divinity and humanity constitute two distinct Persons (Nestorius's view) or are united in a single Person, and, if united, whether in one nature or two.
why_it_mattered: It generated, in Russell's words, 'an almost incredible degree of passion and fury,' split the Eastern and Western Church along roughly the Suez line, and produced a lasting schism (Nestorianism) that spread across Syria, Persia, India, and China, weakening Byzantine control over Syria and facilitating the later Arab conquest.
historical_origin: Came to a head when Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, objected to calling the Virgin Mary 'Mother of God,' since (on his view) she was mother only of the human Person, not the divine Person.
examples: The Council of Ephesus (431), where Western bishops arrived first, locked the doors against late-comers, and condemned Nestorius under Cyril's presidency
competing_positions: Cyril's doctrine of the unity of Christ's person
The Monophysite view (one nature only), later condemned at Chalcedon
influence_on_later_thinkers: Nestorianism became a major missionary church across Asia; the persecution of Nestorians by Constantinople contributed, in Russell's account, to disaffection that assisted the Muslim conquest of Syria.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological and ecclesiastical-political, decided by council votes and imperial and papal backing rather than philosophical argument alone.
